groupRules.bothTitle: It is under ou=groups AND carries a group objectClass. This is what a group written the conventional way looks like.
groupRules.placementTitle: It is under ou=groups but carries no group objectClass. This directory is schemaless, so nothing refused the add — it is listed here because of where it sits.
groupRules.objectClassTitle: It carries a group objectClass but sits outside ou=groups. Nothing here requires a group to live under the groups container.
body.danglingTitle: Membership values naming an entry this directory does not hold. Deleting a user does not remove it from the groups that list it — referential integrity is a directory feature and not a protocol rule, and this directory deliberately does not have it.
body.claimedTitle: Entries whose own memberOf names this group and which this group does not list back. Nothing here maintains memberOf, so a client that writes it creates exactly this disagreement.
body.filterHint: part of a cn or a DN
body.noMatch: No group matches. {filtered, select, yes {The filter above may be hiding some.} other {This directory holds none — the two it seeds can be deleted through the protocol like any other entry.}}
body.whatAGroupIs: A group is an entry that sits under {groupsDn}, or that carries one of the group object classes (groupOfNames, groupOfUniqueNames, posixGroup, groupOfURLs) wherever it sits — either rule is enough, and the column above says which one caught each. Both are applied because this directory is schemaless: nothing stops a client adding a groupOfNames under {usersDn}, or an entry with no objectClass at all under the groups container, and a page that applied only one rule would answer for one of those and quietly lose the other.
body.counts: Members counts the values of member, uniqueMember and memberUid together; Resolve is how many of them name an entry this directory actually holds and Dangling is the rest. The two are shown apart because a group whose seven members resolve to five is this directory doing exactly what it says it does — deleting a user leaves its DN in every group that listed it — and one combined number would report that as seven members with nothing wrong. Claimed is the disagreement in the other direction: entries whose own memberOf names the group while the group does not list them back.
body.createNote: It goes to cn=<what you typed>,{groupsDn} as a groupOfNames, so it is counted here by both rules. Members are one per line or comma-separated, and each may be a user name or any DN — a group can hold another group, and no user name names one. A name with no entry behind it is written as a dangling member rather than refused: this directory does no referential integrity in either direction, and refusing here would make the state the Dangling column reports impossible to produce from this page. Leaving the box empty creates a group with no members, which RFC 4519 says a real directory would refuse and this schemaless one does not.
body.noWriter: No group can be created from here. The list above is read through one slot and the writes through another, and this process has only the first — a build without ldap_server.js's group writer. An ldapadd and POST /scim/v2/Groups are unaffected.
directoryListenerWarning.down: The directory's listeners are not up — {error}. {subject, select, entry {The entry below is in this process's store and is what an LDAP client WOULD read} groups {The groups below are in this process's store and are what an LDAP client WOULD read} other {The group below is in this process's store and is what an LDAP client WOULD read}}; right now no client can connect, most likely because TCP {port} was already taken. This page is HTTP and answers either way.
directoryListenerWarning.plainDown: The directory's plain listener is not up — {error} — but LDAPS on {ldapsPort} is, so {subject, select, entry {the entry below is} groups {the groups below are} other {the group below is}} reachable over TLS. TCP {port} was most likely already taken.
directoryListenerWarning.ldapsDown: The plain listener on {port} is up; LDAPS is not. That affects how {subject, select, entry {the entry below can be reached, not whether it is there} groups {the groups below can be reached, not whether they are there} other {the group below can be reached, not whether it is there}}.
groupsCaveat.grantsNothing: A group here grants nothing, with exactly two exceptions and they are named below. No endpoint in this service checks a group, and nothing in any protocol decides anything on one. Adding somebody to cn=directory-admins changes what a directory client sees, and what a token says, and changes nothing at all about what that token can DO — on a service that authenticates nobody, it could hardly be otherwise.
groupsCaveat.exceptionsBefore: The two exceptions are {read} and {write}, which decide who may use THIS CONSOLE — see
groupsCaveat.exceptionsAfter: , where they are granted and taken away. They are ordinary groups and appear in the table above like any other, deliberately: the alternative was a membership store of the console's own that an ldapmodify could not see. Even those two grant nothing outside /admin — no token, assertion, ticket, PAC or credential is changed by being in one, and every protocol endpoint answers a member exactly as it answers anybody else.
groupsCaveat.claimBefore: A token can now carry one. With groups.claim on — it is on by default — every OAuth 2.0 access token, OIDC ID Token, SAML 2.0 assertion and SAML 1.1 assertion this service issues carries a claim naming the groups its subject is in, read from these entries at the moment it is minted. Somebody in no group gets no claim at all rather than an empty list. What it is called, whether each value is a cn or a whole DN, and whether a person's own memberOf counts are the four settings at the foot of this page;
groupsCaveat.claimAfter: shows what it would say about one person. No Kerberos PAC and no WS-Federation-specific token carries a group either way.
groupsLinks.users: the people who have authenticated here
detail.notAGroup: There is an entry at {entryDn}, and it is not a group: it sits outside {groupsDn} and carries no group objectClass. A modifyDN out of the groups container or a modify that deleted the objectClass does exactly this, and neither is refused — this directory has no schema.
detail.nothingAt: Nothing is at {wanted}. Either it was deleted or modifyDN’d through the protocol since the link was drawn, or the DN was typed. DNs are compared case-folded and with the space after each comma ignored, so the spelling is not what is wrong.
detail.danglingTitle: The value names an entry this directory does not hold. It is shown rather than dropped: nothing here enforces referential integrity, so this is the state the protocol leaves behind when a member is deleted.
detail.claimedHeading: Entries that claim this group, and that it does not list
detail.claimedNote: Each of these carries a memberOf naming this group while this group’s own member does not name them back. Nothing here maintains memberOf — it is not a standard attribute at all (Microsoft’s directory and OpenLDAP’s memberof overlay both write it, the server keeping it in step with member itself), and a schemaless mock that neither writes nor checks it lets a client create exactly this disagreement in one modify. They are listed apart from the members above rather than merged into them, because which side of the disagreement a name came from is the only interesting thing about it.
detail.timestamps: The two timestamps are generalized time (YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ), which is what a directory shows — not the ISO 8601 strings the rest of this console uses. An LDAP client bound to ldap://<host>:{port} reading {dn} sees exactly the object below, because it is that object and not a copy of it.
detail.empty: This group lists nobody. An empty groupOfNames is something a real directory refuses — RFC 4519 makes member MUST — and this one has no schema, so it is here because something wrote it.
detail.membershipRead: Membership is read from {attributes}. The first two hold a DN; memberUid holds a bare user name, which is looked up under {usersDn} — treating the three alike is how a page ends up reporting every posixGroup member as dangling. Nesting is shown and not expanded: a member that is itself a group links to its own page, and nobody inside it is counted here, because nothing in this service walks a group tree and a flattened list would be claiming a feature that is not here.
detail.usersColumn: The last column links to the users page only for somebody this service has actually seen authenticate. The other members are marked never here, and that is not a fault: the directory holds whatever somebody wrote into it — the three people it seeds at startup, and anything a client has added since — while the users page holds whoever has presented a credential to this process. alice is in this directory from the moment it starts and appears on the users page only once somebody signs in as her. A link that was always drawn would usually land on “nothing here has authenticated as alice”, which reads as a broken link rather than as the answer it is.
detail.addBefore: The value written is that person’s OWN entry wherever it is — somebody whose entry was seeded by a client certificate is at cn=<name>,{usersDn} and not at uid=, and a membership written in the wrong form would dangle beside the entry it was meant to name. With nobody there yet, the uid= form is written, so the value resolves the moment they authenticate. It goes onto member whatever else this entry carries, and adding somebody already listed changes nothing and says so. Taking one out is not here: it is an ldapmodify or a SCIM PATCH, and
detail.addAfter: for the two groups that grant this console.
detail.attributesNote: The whole object, operational attributes included — a search returns those only when they are asked for by name (RFC 4511 §4.5.1.8), and this is a dump rather than a search. The membership attributes are in here too, as the raw values the store holds; the table above is the same values resolved. This directory is schemaless: no objectClass is enforced and no value is checked against a syntax, so an attribute a real directory would refuse is here because something wrote it.
usersPageCell.noNameTitle: This entry is not named uid=<name> and carries no uid, so there is no name to look it up by. The console files people under the local name userFor() derives; an entry named some other way — a cn=, or the one a TLS client certificate seeds — has none.
usersPageCell.neverHereTitle: The directory holds an entry for them and nothing has authenticated as this name in this process, so the users page has no row to link to. The two lists answer different questions: the directory is what somebody wrote into it, the users page is who has actually presented a credential here.
attributeTable.operationalTitle: An operational attribute. A search returns it only when it is asked for by name (RFC 4511 section 4.5.1.8) — this dump shows it always.
